slides.html: 1. The Language of Exchange Rates
slides.title: 1. The Language of Exchange Rates

slides.html:
Quotes and changes

  • e= the home-currency price of one unit of foreign currency; a rise in e = depreciation
  • bid/ask: the bank's bid < ask; reciprocals swap the two ends
  • log change \Delta s=\ln(e_1/e_0): additive, symmetric
  • A rise in an effective-rate index = appreciation, the opposite of e

Example: e 7.20 → 7.56: depreciation of 5% (log 4.88%).
slides.title: Quotes and changes

slides.html:
The real exchange rate

q=eP^*/P; a rise = real depreciation of the home currency.

Example: nominal depreciation 2.2%, foreign inflation 2%, home inflation 5%: \Delta q\approx2.2+2-5=-0.8\%.

The nominal depreciation was eaten by home inflation; competitiveness falls.
slides.title: The real exchange rate

slides.html: 2. Covered Interest Parity (CIP)
slides.title: 2. Covered Interest Parity (CIP)

slides.html:
A quote that violates CIP: how arbitrage pays

Suppose F=7.25 (above 7.1644), per 7.20 of principal:

  1. borrow 7.20 CNY, repay 7.2360 after 3 months
  2. convert to 1 USD, deposit: 1.01 USD
  3. sell forward at 7.25: 7.3225 CNY
  4. profit 0.0865 CNY, riskless

Arbitrageurs buy spot and sell forward; F returns to 7.1644.
slides.title: A quote that violates CIP: how arbitrage pays

slides.html:
Using CIP

  1. Forward points = the interest differential, not "the market is bearish"
  2. A hedged foreign bond earns the home rate (A: 2%)
  3. A forward hedge = "buying" the differential with forward points
  4. An FX swap = borrowing one currency against another

The forward rate is not a forecast; it is the price of an interest differential.
slides.title: Using CIP

slides.html:
CIP deviations and the cross-currency basis

i^{imp}=\tfrac1\tau\Big[\tfrac Fe(1+i^*\tau)-1\Big],\qquad x=i^{imp}-i
  • Persistent deviations since 2008 (Du–Tepper–Verdelhan 2018)
  • Cause: bank balance-sheet constraints, dollar funding stress
  • A wider basis \approx global dollar funding stress

Example: F=7.15: i^{imp}=1.19\%, basis -81 basis points.
slides.title: CIP deviations and the cross-currency basis

slides.html: 3. Uncovered Interest Parity (UIP) and the Carry Trade
slides.title: 3. Uncovered Interest Parity (UIP) and the Carry Trade

slides.html:
UIP: expected depreciation offsets the differential

\frac{E[e_{t+\tau}]-e_t}{e_t}\approx(i-i^*)\tau

Assumptions: risk neutrality + rational expectations + no costs.

i=5\%, i^*=2\%: the home currency is expected to depreciate about 3% a year.

If CIP and UIP both hold: F_t=E_t[e_{t+\tau}].
slides.title: UIP: expected depreciation offsets the differential

slides.html:
The Fama regression, step by step

s_{t+1}-s_t=\alpha+\beta(f_t-s_t)+\varepsilon_{t+1}
  1. get monthly spot s_t and 1-month forward f_t (logs)
  2. y=s_{t+1}-s_t, x=f_t-s_t
  3. OLS gives \hat\beta
  4. overlapping samples: Newey–West standard errors
  5. test \beta=1 (UIP) and \beta=0
slides.title: The Fama regression, step by step

slides.html:
Fama decomposition: what \beta<0 means

f_t-s_t=E[\Delta s]+rp_t (expected depreciation + risk premium)

\beta=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(E\Delta s)+\operatorname{Cov}(E\Delta s,rp)}{\operatorname{Var}(f-s)}

\beta<0: the risk premium is large and variable and moves against expected depreciation.
slides.title: Fama decomposition: what \beta<0 means
The carry trade: up the stairs, down the elevator

slides.html:
Using UIP in macro analysis

  • Differential = expected depreciation + risk premium
  • A hike: spot appreciation, then expected depreciation (overshooting, Ch. 8)
  • Do not use UIP to forecast
  • High differentials often come with larger crash risk
slides.title: Using UIP in macro analysis

slides.html:
CIP and UIP side by side

CIP UIP
Nature no-arbitrage identity assumption about expectations
Assumptions no costs, no controls risk neutrality + rational expectations
Profit? riskless, vanishes at once risky, may pay on average
Evidence held before 2008, deviations since fails systematically
slides.title: CIP and UIP side by side

slides.html: 4. Purchasing Power Parity
slides.title: 4. Purchasing Power Parity

slides.html:
PPP and the real exchange rate

  • Absolute PPP: e=P/P^*; relative PPP: \Delta\ln e\approx\pi-\pi^*
  • Example: basket 200 yuan / 25 dollars: PPP rate 8.00; q=7.20\times25/200=0.90: overvalued by about 10%
  • Balassa–Samuelson: rich countries have higher price levels; catching-up economies' real rates appreciate as a trend
  • PPP puzzle: mean reversion is slow (half-life 3–5 years)

Use: compare q with its mean to judge misalignment, not to forecast.
slides.title: PPP and the real exchange rate

slides.html: 5. The Balance of Payments and the Income Identity
slides.title: 5. The Balance of Payments and the Income Identity

slides.html:
The identity: deficit = saving gap

CA=(S^p-I)+(T-G)

Y=100,C=70,I=25,G=20,T=18: NX=-15; private -13; government -2.

An identity is not causation; ask what the borrowing did and how it is financed.
slides.title: The identity: deficit = saving gap

slides.html:
Net foreign assets: where a deficit accumulates to

b^*=\frac{ca}{g}

Country A: ca=-3\%, g=6\%: b^*=-50\%.

Deficit 5%, growth 4%: b^*=-125\%: financing difficulties almost certain.
slides.title: Net foreign assets: where a deficit accumulates to

slides.html:
The checklist

Question Indicators
What do prices say? differential, forward points, CIP basis
Is the currency misaligned? q, REER vs mean
How are the external accounts? CA/GDP, b^*=ca/g, financing structure
Will depreciation help? elasticities, J-curve, capacity
Is there policy space? trilemma: which two sides?
What is the worst case? foreign debt, short-term debt/reserves
slides.title: The checklist

slides.html:
Case A: the US raises rates by 3 percentage points

  • differential +2\to-1; 3-month forward 7.182: the dollar moves from premium to discount
  • foreign-currency debt 15% of GDP: a 10% depreciation adds 1.5\% of GDP to the debt burden
  • reserves 25% / short-term external debt 10% = 2.5 times

Conclusion: moderate hikes + some depreciation + push firms to hedge.
slides.title: Case A: the US raises rates by 3 percentage points

slides.html:
Cases B and C

B: does a 3% deficit matter? b^*=-50\%; look at financing structure and use; with g=4\%, -75\%.

C: can a fixed-rate country cut rates? Outflows \Rightarrow sell reserves \Rightarrow withdraw money: no, unless it abandons the peg or imposes capital controls.
slides.title: Cases B and C

slides.html:
Common misconceptions

Misconception Correct
The forward rate is a forecast It is the price of the differential (CIP)
A hedged high-yield foreign bond still earns the spread The hedged return = the home rate
UIP forecasts exchange rates It fails systematically in the data
A rise in e = appreciation A rise in e = depreciation
Depreciation always improves the balance Needs the elasticity condition; J-curve first
A deficit = a loss A deficit = net borrowing; look at the use
slides.title: Common misconceptions
